articles.title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America
articles.summary: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America

top_comments: I use a kei truck for farming. They are incredibly pragmatic little vehicles. They are very capable driving around on dirt/gravel agricultural roads with 4WD, and they are inexpensive and robust enough that you can really beat them up and use them as a tool without worry. Repairs and replacement parts are ubiquitous and inexpensive. Having the sides of bed fold down is also really useful.They aren't comfortable to drive at all (although just having A/C at all on a hot summer day in the field is a godsend), and I wouldn't want to do longer trips in one - although you certainly could in a pinch.It seems like Toyota/Scion is just testing the waters here, and I'm not sure how successful they'll be. But I hope there is a future for kei trucks in the US.

25 mph works for golf courses, resort, or island use. In rural areas on the mainland, roads connecting towns often have 45 or 55 mph speed limits so unless you plan on staying on the farm I don't think these are practical for trips to go shopping, dumping, hauling, etc.As for the imports, I saw one of these 90s-era right-hand drive kei trucks at a parking lot a few months ago and talked with the owner. He was a young guy who lived in Boston, said it was super easy to park. Speed maxed out at 70 mph, which is fine for local trips but maybe not for long highway trips.For people in jurisdictions that allow 30 year old truck imports, and are interested in getting one, there are other countries that use such trucks and have left-hand drive. Taiwan has models from CMC and Suzuki, and I believe South Korea also makes them.

With a built in 25mph limiter, that eliminates "city" driving too unfortunately. Most roads around me are 35 mph.There's sizeable demand for people who want to be able to do runs to the bigbox stores for garden and DIY renovation supplies and store it the rest of the time.

articles.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
articles.summary: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers

top_comments: > If you fail to comply with our demands by the specified deadline, Synaptics will seek monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts.Obviously this is intended as a scare tactic, but, surely that could never hold up in court? Surely the burden of proof is on the owner of the patents to prove that someone's work is infringing, and you can't then say "We are charging the defendant to prove that we have a valid case against them." ?

> I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts.There is no universe in which this is a reasonable response.

DisplayLink is dying due to high DDR prices. Dock companies are cancelling their display link portfolios due to the unfavorable economics.Good riddance if this is how OSS is treated by synaptics.Most recent thunderbolt docks and usb4 docks have good display support, and fallback to DisplayPort alt mode if the host does not support tbt4. Which is much better supported over type-c. Intel and AMD upstream host support.

I remember Steve from my days working on Eve, he was part of that community and always a big proponent of end-user programming. I was happy to see him working on this project but am not surprised it's shutting down.Nothing to to do with the quality of Val Town, but making a business in this space is really, really hard. You can't start the business without raising millions (Eve raised $2M, Darklang raised $3.5M, Val Town raised $7M), but it's hard to scale out a proof of concept in the time investors want to start seeing an ROI. It seems to me about 2-3 years is all you get for seed runway, when realistically projects like this should take at minimum 5 years incubating. Darklang extended their runway to ~7-8 years by firing all the devs and keeping just the founder on life support. Ultimately even that wasn't enough.But maybe with AI this could work, I dunno.What's required to make it all work is a fundamental leap in programming interface design, but the business side doesn't look any different from a typical SaaS. So unless you hit the ball out of the park you're entering the market with an experimental product, then you have to deal with product-market fit even if you have the right product, so you really only have one shot.It's very hard to go back to investors and ask for another round of funding when there's no discernable market and the product isn't gaining the traction investors would like to see.Anyway, kudos to Steve for fighting the good fight! What would really be great is to read an in-depth post mortem on the project. Looking forward to it if you have time!

Not mentioned directly in the blog post, but Val Town was fundamentally organized around the Deno runtime, whose team will stop maintaining it next year after joining Cloudflare [0].[0] https://deno.com/blog/cloudflare

This is sad. We're in a similar space as Val Town (which technically made us competitors) but I've always appreciated the care they had for the craft and the values they drove forward as a company like their transparency (even their investor updates were public).Steve and Tom also individually have some of the best blogs out on the web.I wish them all the best with whatever comes next. I'm pretty sure they'll all do great things.

articles.title: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings
articles.summary: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings

top_comments: I received 9 reports of Fil-C issues from AnthropicAll of them were real bugs. None of them were false positives.The quality of the reports was exceptional. (My baseline is doing security defense on a browser engine, so my baseline has a large sample count and is probably representative of what experts are capable of.)The quality of the proposed fixes was alright. I took some of the fixes verbatim. I used most of the fixes as significant inspiration for doing it my way.The quality of the test cases was exceptional.Maybe I’m special somehow! But I just want to call out the enormous chasm between what I saw of anthropic’s capability and what TFA says

As someone working at a bigtech co that has spent every single working day (and many weekends) since the launch of Mythos patching serious, company-ending type of security issues, these types of posts really irk me.Public datasets of CVEs being underwhelming doesn't mean much if all of the issues are in private company codebases that will never get a CVE number assigned and will never get a fancy blog post. You're never going to hear about them, and the people working on them probably can't tell you about them, but that doesn't mean they don't exist.We're all worried about OSS having security issues because of how widely used things like PHP or curl are... but the same can be said about email providers, document collaboration SaaSes, payment processors, etc that millions of companies depend. Those companies will never be in datasets like this, and they'll never publicly disclose how many issues they found.

The PHP2Shell vulnerability ended up being paradoxically comforting for me.They turned frontier models loose on PHP, and the big one they found was based on a previously known logic flaw that was extremely difficult to exploit. Which makes sense: hence the need for frontier models.And in the wild, while there have been many attempts and a few simple demo successes, the practical impact has seemed to be small, seemingly constrained by the length of the chain and the diversity of PHP configs.In short, it was indeed a major vulnerability, but not magic (in the Arthur C Clarke sense).I think ultimately the fear comes down to: do you believe that code can be secured. I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc. But if one believes code can be constructed to operate to spec, then there must be a limit to the damage an LLM can do, even a very smart one.I think we are going through a phase where a lot of known triaged code shortcomings will get exposed and hopefully fixed. Sucks while it is happening. But not actually the first round of this type of evolution. And ultimately I think as before, we will come out the other side with more secure and durable technology.

articles.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
articles.summary: Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without s everywhere, `` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0])Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent +JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.Try it out: DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1---0: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=504164561: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/guides2: https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/

top_comments: Here's a list of browser features the skills will tell your agent to use that are stable in Chrome but not supported by Firefox and Safari: CSS @function CSS calc-size() CSS interpolate-size CSS corner-shape CSS border-shape CSS flex-wrap: balance CSS text-fit CSS text-decoration-skip-spaces CSS scroll-axis-lock CSS scroll-target-group CSS :target-current CSS scroll-initial-target CSS container scroll-state queries scrollsnapchange event scrollsnapchanging event HTML focusgroup Element.startViewTransition() CSS view-transition-scope Interest Invokers (interestfor) LanguageModel (Prompt API) LanguageDetector Translator Summarizer API Window.fetchLater() Speculation Rules API Long Animation Frames API VisibilityStateEntry PerformanceSoftNavigation InteractionContentfulPaint Connection-Allowlist CSS url() integrity() modifier HTML meta name="text-scale" HTML template for HTML processing instructions PasswordCredential Promise-returning scroll methods Web App Origin Migration Local Network Access permissions Request.targetAddressSpace beforeinstallprompt event To be fair, the skills also recommend ~11 features not supported by Chrome itself. And the project does seem concerned with compatibility: "Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks."

Distribution suggestion: in addition to the npm packages you have right now, set up GitHub Pages to publish a markdown index document of the skills at https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/skill... (currently a 404)That index page should link to plain markdown versions of all of the documents, and should be designed for search with grep to find the right answers.That way I don't have to install anything at all - provided my agent has the ability to make HTTP requests I can tell it "Look for tips on https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/skill..." and it will fetch the index, then navigate to the most relevant documents - no MCP or npm or installation required at all.

> If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!But how? Hopefully filing an issue on the modern-web-guidance-src repo is the right place? Anyway I filed one for using fromBase64 and toBase64 instead of atob and btoa.But since you're all in on agents anyway you should consider having one look through at least all of the JS, DOM, and HTML spec commits in the last 3-5 years and automatically triaging any that are clear improvements and are not used by agents. Would be pretty straightforward.---Btw, I think it would be very helpful to automatically provide versions of this depending on what browsers you're targeting. I don't want to use anything that hasn't been available in all evergreen browsers for at least a year, for example; I think most developers have a similar standard, or at the very least don't want to use the bleeding edge. And while it is _possible_ to get that from your repo, it takes some effort, either writing a script or letting the agent use its own judgement for every feature. That's work you could do on your end and save the rest of us from needing to.

articles.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
articles.summary: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast

top_comments: The worst thing about consumer (AM5) Zen4 and Zen5 is the I/O die chiplet and memory controller on it. I've heard they're finally going to ship a new I/O chiplet in Zen6 on a much smaller node. Their existing AM5 Zen4/5 memory controller when using both memory channels is terrible. Extremely hard or impossible to get above 3600 MT/s.Of all the things I'm looking forward to on Zen6, an improved memory controller is at the top of the list.Edit: and yes, others may say the paltry few PCIE 5.0 lanes is the worst thing about AM5, but that doesn't affect my usage much, and unfortunately I think that's a limitation of AM5 itself rather than the I/O chiplet.

The instruction level parallelism in the 2-ahead branch prediction is super cool stuff, I know zen5 had this feature but it's kind of crazy that memory is so slow relative to the cores that this complexity is beneficial and worthwhile.

> AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two.Are PDEP and PEXT using the same (parts of) circuits as multiply (they are very different operations...), or are this just two independent drops of circuitry and the wording is just a bit unclear?
